title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Eris/Hel
content:
First released in plastic in the Core Box, the Eris is a new take on being a simple trooper medium mech. Like the Griffin or Wolverine, it’s got adequate mobility, armor, and firepower – armor is let down slightly by being 50 tons instead of the classic 55 ton trooper, but it’s still more than adequate. It’s got an interesting backstory, as it was first created as the Hel by an industrial mech manufacturer expanding into battlemechs, but they ended up selling the specifications elsewhere when they were unable to get buyers. Strange, since this is a pretty good mech. Amusingly, as record sheets do exist for the Hel, it can be used as a work-around in a tournament that limits you to only having a single copy of a mech variant – the Eris ERS-2N and Hel HL-1 are identical in all but name.

Jade Falcon Eris. Credit: Jack Hunter

Chassis

The Eris is a 50 ton medium mech with all three variants moving 5/8/5 or 5/8/7 with a partial wing. It’s a straightforward design, an XL engine, endo-steel structure, and standard armor combine to give it enough crit slots for a decent armament while not being excessively limited on tonnage. Armor layout is good, everything is armored past the key 15-pip breakpoint, and at 22 armor the legs aren’t getting taken off too easily. I do wish that the rear side torsos had 6 pips of armor instead of 5, but I don’t think there’s anywhere I’d pull armor away from to make that happen.

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

Broken Arrows Eris ERS-2N. Credit: Valk

ERS-2H

A heavy PPC, paired ER medium lasers, and a streak SRM 6 rack give this the ability to do a little bit of everything, even if it doesn’t excel at anything. The XL engine renders it vulnerable to torso destruction, but it’s fully armored so that’s not a big concern to me – it’s still going to take enough firepower to bring down that you’ll usually get good value out of it. At 1,674 BV it makes a great filler unit for a force, especially as the left arm has hand actuators, useful for any Core Rules missions that use mobile objectives.

Jack’s Rating: B

ERS-2N

Superficially similar to the 2H, the 2N adds a partial wing to boost mobility up to 5/8/7, and swaps the weapon load out for a snub-nose PPC, pair of MML 5s, and trio of small x-pulse lasers. While it does go up four heat on a run, you’re not usually going to be firing the PPC and small pulses at the same time, and only going up four still leaves you below any heat penalties if you do need to. It also only goes up one heat on a full jump with snub + MMLs (or neutral with pulse + MMLs), so you can jump and fire reasonably effectively (not that jumping and firing will have you hitting much). Generally I think this is a more useful weapon load than the 2H. You do lose out on the headcap potential from the heavy PPC, but you’ve got more missile tubes, can pack them with infernos or acid SRMs, and the small pulses give you a bit more ability to deal with light harassers. It’s also a drop down to 1,400 BV, making it easier to fit into a list.

Jack’s Rating: B+

Eris. Credit: Jack Hunter

ERS-3R

Normally I’d call this some periphery bullshit, but it appears to be made solely by the Free Worlds League. Like the 2N it has a partial wing for 5/8/7 mobility, and actually picks up an extra nine points of armor. It does have three ER medium lasers, but most of the armament is the 24 rocket launcher 10s it carries. Mostly I think you fire two of these per turn along with your medium lasers while keeping an eye out for anything that falls down and can’t get up, shuts down, passes out, or is otherwise immobilized – and then you have two choices. Either unload everything, probably trading the Eris for their mech, or skip your lasers to fire 12 of the rocket launchers. In the first situation, you’ve got 89 heat, and sinking 23 per turn will take three turns before you even have a chance to turn on again. In the second you’ll go up to 15 heat, only needing to avoid shutdown on a 4+, and can jump away the next turn. I don’t really think either is a strategy you want to count on for winning games, and 1,868 BV is way more than I’d pay for this, but it’s pretty funny.

Jack’s Rating: D+

Hel HL-1

As mentioned in the intro, this is identical in every way except the name to the Eris ERS-2H. It’s got a different entry on MUL, so it can dodge around chassis/variant limitations in an event.

Hel HL-2

The Hl-2 swaps the heavy PPC of the ERS-2H/HL-1 for a pair of large lasers. I’m neutral on this swap – it’s more theoretical damage, higher chance to put at least some damage through, and gets rid of the awkward minimum range that overlaps with your SRMs. On the other hand, putting out a 15 point hit is very useful. It’s 1,549 BV and compares very closely to the Starslayer STY-3C. I would generally start out with the ERS-2H in my list, but if I need that hundred-odd BV I’ll swap down to the HL-2 without complaint.

Jack’s Rating: B

Hastati Sentinels Eris. Credit: Jack Hunter

Conclusion

It’s a very simple mech that’s hard to go wrong with. The rocket variant is much more funny than good, which is pretty typical, but all three of the other variants make for good simple troopers. Take whichever one you have BV available for and you’ll get an easy to use reliable mech.

title: Eberron creator Keith Baker talks Daggerheart, D&D, and the freedom of his new, ghostly fantasy setting
content:
Keith Baker, best known for designing the beloved D&D setting Eberron just funded a new venture. His publishing house, Twogether Studios, just raised almost $122,000 for a new Daggerheart campaign book. Co-created by Baker and Jenn Ellis, Eidolon: The Ghost Market is a ghost-powered fantasy city that revels in the strange and unusual.

I for one think the world sounds intriguing, and it's a strong fit for Daggerheart's narrative-led heroic fantasy rules. I'm not here to sell it to you though; Baker does a more than adequate job in our recent interview. He also has some pretty insightful things to say about the design philosophies of both D&D and Daggerheart, as well as the continued legacy of Eberron. Check it out:

WG: Give me an elevator pitch for Eidolon as a setting

KB: One of the things I loved when creating Eberron was looking at the impact magic would have on a culture. Eidolon is a city where necromancy, specifically the binding of ghosts, is a cornerstone of their industry and technology. For weapons and armor, you're sort of wearing a ghost who protects you or enhances your senses, or things like that.

I like to say it's a bit of a blend between Sweeney Todd, Dracula, and Neuromancer. You're playing people in a system that crushes those at the bottom. The city is ruled by five oligarch families that control the necromantic industry, and they're all terrible in their own way. They run a system where your ghost is the most valuable thing you own.

Some people compare it to Blades in the Dark, and there are similarities. But I would say Blades is much darker, whereas a key point of Eidolon is trying to find hope. You're trying to find justice or vengeance, or just make a difference.

With our sourcebook, you can do whatever you want with the setting. It describes the factions, the houses, and the districts, but it also contains two campaign frames.

The first, Boneriggers, is the Sweeney Todd path. Part of it involves deciding which of the five houses is an enemy your party seeks vengeance against. But, beyond that driving force, you also decide the community that binds your team together. As the campaign unfolds, you're doing mercenary work and investigations as part of your vengeance quest, but they impact your community.

The other path is called Catering Crew, and it's more of a wild heist. You're essentially catering parties in the mansions of the oligarchs, some of the worst and most dangerous people in Eidolon, and you're trying to accomplish goals under their noses. It's a little more whimsical, and it's a bit like crazy, evil Bridgerton - or like catering a party for Sauron or Darth Vader.

What interests me about Eidolon is its preoccupation with the past. We have magic items literally built by bonding a ghost to it - and you mentioned that happy ghosts don't stick around.

This is a society that requires misery to function. Why was that a story you thought it was important to tell?

Eidolon was built at the site of a gate to the underworld, so you can talk to people on the other side, and it's this intensely haunted area where ghosts linger easily. The idea was, rather than presenting your typical D&D necromancy with zombies and skeletons, we consider why ghosts linger.

Ghosts linger because of trauma, unfinished business, or intense emotion, and they're not continuously conscious. This is mechanically baked into the system, and what you can do with a ghost is based on the emotion driving it. Poltergeists are driven by anger and move things, while Miseries are despair, and they affect emotion and perception. Specters observe, and muses remember.

Once that ghost is bound [to a magic item], there's nothing cruel about using it. When your armor holds the spirit of a dead lover who protects you, most of the time they're sort of asleep.

What is cruel is the system this exists in. The ruling houses are going to work you to death. They want you to be angry and miserable, because that's what creates ghosts. That's their crime, and that's what really makes them monsters. Living well really is the best revenge here, and that's how you break down a system that's making everybody miserable.

It sounds like Eidolon lends itself well to Daggerheart. A lot of that RPG system revolves around this struggle between hope and fear, light and dark, levity and grit.

Exactly. Eidolon is an idea we've had kicking around for about 10 years - we actually made a Fiasco set using it. And now, we're making a different setting with Daggerheart in future, so we wanted to warm up and get to know the system. Eidolon was sitting around, not doing anything, and we felt it fit with Daggerheart. This is a city shaped by fear, but you're the people holding on to hope.

Plus, at its core, Daggerheart is not a wargame. You can later whatever story you want onto Dungeons and Dragons, but it is a wargame. That's where it began, and it's weird running D&D with no combat whatsoever. In Daggerheart, the combat is equally weighted with social interaction.

The Catering Crew campaign frame, in particular, has a good half to two thirds that's just managing a party. You could tell that story in Dungeons and Dragons, but it's not the story the mechanics want to tell.

I feel like this current era of D&D really pushes the idea that the system can do everything and anything - but I firmly believe the mechanics tell the stories they want to tell, regardless of your plans.

100%. You can tell any story with D&D, because you can tell any story with anything, but the system has things it wants to do. If you're playing D&D, where two thirds of your character sheet is combat abilities, and there's no combat or conflict, it feels wasted.

I would love to see a module for D&D - and I've thought about doing this occasionally - that's designed for social conflict. What I mean is actually going through the classes and saying 'oh, the Barbarian can throw a tantrum', or the Rogue's class abilities are more about being sneaky. Daggerheart's social conflicts have as much weight as its combat, and that fits well with Eidolon, where action and conflict are very much part of it, but that's not all there is to it.

What else attracted you to Daggerheart as a designer?

First off, I love Eberron and I'm going to keep supporting it. But Eberron is D&D. It has to be D&D legally, so I've already got a D&D setting to work on. With Daggerheart, we wanted to try a new setting, and why not make it in a new system? Why not explore something else?

Secondly, Daggerheart embraces the way I like to run any roleplaying game. I really like pulling out the collaborative storytelling aspect. One of the simple things I've always done in D&D is, if you run into a mob of zombies, I'll make each player describe one of the zombies. That really draws players into a story and helps them visualize it in a concrete way. Daggerheart leans into that and makes it part of the core philosophy.

It is fair to say, in a small way, Eidolon grew from the fact you can't work on Eberron in the ways you might like?

Absolutely. It's the whole reason I have a game company. We make card games and board games as well as roleplaying games, and I've even written novels, but I can't do that in Eberron now for legal reasons. I can't write a new Eberron novel or make an Eberron card game. We wanted to make something we can explore down any avenue we like.

I'm very happy and grateful to Wizards that they made the DM's Guild. Phoenix Dawn Command came out because, 10 years prior to that, there was no way to create Eberron content. I love the fact that I can now create in the setting through that specific channel - and so can other people. There's 1,000 Eberron products on the DM's Guild, and I love that.

I wanted a setting where I had the freedom to do more, but I'm at least glad Wizards have opened Eberron up in that way. They could have just sat on it and kept the vault closed.

You're the originator of Eberron, but you've shared authorship of the world with so many people, from other designers and publishers to fans creating their own content. What are the ups and downs of that?

First of all, I want to give credit where credit is due. The core concept of Eberron started with me as part of Wizards' fantasy setting search. But even from the very beginning, Wizards sat me in a room with James Wyatt, Chris Perkins, and Bill Slavicsek. We all worked together, adding and removing pieces from the idea.

A lot of people helped shape Eberron in key ways. I've stuck with it and continued to push elements that were important to me. But even the name Eberron is actually Bill Slavicsek's name. I call myself the creator of Eberron because it did begin with me, but a lot of people put their spin on it.

Going back to the philosophy of Daggerheart, I've always said Eberron is a source of inspiration, not something that restricts the stories you want to tell. I grew up doing homebrew, reading the core rules and taking ideas from there. I want people to take what they like and change the things they don't. Don't let canon stop you because one part doesn't fit the story you want to tell.

Not everybody has to make their own world, and some people like to share a common foundation with everyone, but I've always said 'make it your own'. My books on the DM's Guild aren't canon, and I sometimes contradict the canon and do things my way. I don't agree with all the writers who've ever written for Eberron, and you don't have to either.

I have wanted to write D&D books since I was 14. I knew what I wanted to do, but I never expected to make something that so many people would get to experience and share. I love seeing people explore it and make it their own.

Want to chat more about Daggerheart or Dungeons and Dragons? We're always keen to talk nerdy in the official Wargamer Discord.

title: How to get cheap Pokémon cards from Walmart lotteries
content:
Finding Pokémon cards below their sky-high market prices is never easy, and while it's far from a guaranteed method, one option that's well worth knowing about is the regular Walmart lotteries.

Rather than a painful queuing system or a chaotic scramble, Walmart has found a smoother way to dole out a relatively small amount of product to us hordes of desperate Pokémon card collectors.

It runs weekly lotteries, where a small number of customers will be selected and given the option to buy products, within a certain predetermined window. These are often very good deals, with products priced at half what you'll find them for on third party sites like TCGPlayer.

All you need to do is sign up for a Walmart account and have your card details saved. Then, during a predetermined drawing window, you must log on and select the products you're trying to buy.

These windows are a few hours long and take place mid-week in the afternoon. For instance, right now the next drawing entry window is Nov 12, 2:00pm - 3:00pm PST.

By selecting these products, you're authorizing Walmart to make a payment with your saved card details. So you can sit back and wait to see if you're chosen.

The Walmart Pokémon lotteries run every week, so while your chances aren't good on each individual attempt, if you're persistent you may eventually bag yourself a bargain. And you don't pay anything if you're not picked - this isn't gambling.

Share your best pulls over on the Wargamer Discord!

title: Veil of Ashes first impressions - this debut strategy game is pure fire
content:
Veil of Ashes is in a very early, pre-alpha state, and it's already one of the most visually stunning strategy games I've seen in years. First-time developer Greifenmaer revealed a playable demo at the Games Ground convention in Berlin, Germany this weekend, and thanks to an invitation from publisher Slitherine Software I was able to get my hands on it. This one could be special.

Veil of Ashes is set in an alternate timeline: in 1704 a great inferno burns away the familiar nations of earth but leaves behind a powerful new energy source, cinium. New empires and new technologies arise, principally massive steam tanks. Cue catastrophic world wars, and a fantastic premise for a videogame.

There's a very grand sense of scale in Veil of Ashes. Units range from feeble infantry, through light and heavy tanks, up to monumental Behemoths, rolling fortresses with turning circles like oil tankers and the firepower to delete whole battalions. The build I played had no way to summon these things in organically, but I watched a pair of devs cut loose with the cheat menu and spawn them with abandon. Opposing gods of war obliterated one another in the centre of the map with apocalyptic firepower, and it was glorious.

Said map is already fairly deformable: trees crumple under tank treads, artillery shells leave impact creators, and the hulls of destroyed tanks create new obstacles and cover for other troops. I was informed that there are plans to allow infantry to garrison buildings, though this system, as well as embarking on transports, wasn't implemented in the build. And of course there are plans to make buildings destructible.

Even without these features, Veil of Ashes is a fireworks show of destruction. Shells deflect from armor with red hot flashes of light, tank engines cook off in fireballs when shells hit home, and the artillery strikes are art. You can pull the camera back far enough to watch the parabola of each shell, leading a trail of smoke skywards before plummeting down towards its target. A direct hit lands like the judgment of god - zoom in close enough and the screen shakes while a column of fire and shrapnel launches into the air.

I played a couple of trial games, one against a human opponent and one with an AI ally against a pair of computer-controlled foes. Both missions were simple enough exercises in capturing and holding strategic points; a single player campaign is promised, but that's a long way off.

This is a real time tactics game rather than real time strategy, so there's no base building, just a recruitment menu that lets you order up units and deploy them via airship. You have a budget of a basic requisition resource to invest in your troops, which returns to your bank once they're destroyed; heavier tanks require the investment of the rarer resource cinium.

The battlefields are big - not Broken Arrow big, but big - and maneuvering troops means committing them to a journey they can't easily reposition from. When forces clash the engagements are often decisive, though if you manage to retreat a unit you can heal it in a friendly zone.

Infantry are maneuverable but fragile - the devs say they're planning to let them hide in forest cover to reccy or ambush the enemy, but that wasn't in the build yet - and tanks behave just like tanks, either light and fast or heavy and slow.

Artillery pieces are a blast (pun accidental, but I chose not to delete it), with truly massive attack distances. They don't target individual units - instead you'll pick a zone for them to strike. It takes time for a shell to land, during which time your opponent might have repositioned, but a direct hit from even a light artillery piece is devastating. Reconnaissance with faster moving troops is essential for actually locating the enemy, and firing on a hotly contested target zone risks friendly fire.

The build was fairly light on micro-management. Vehicles have stronger and weaker armor facings, so turning the enemy flank is worthwhile, and quite achievable on the huge battlefields; units have different stances and infantry squads can clump up or spread out, features I didn't touch. You need to call in artillery strikes manually from each vehicle; the devs say they're working on the ability to group activate artillery vehicles, and I'd welcome the option to set a fire zone your artillery to continually bombard.

Much remains to be implemented, but Veil of Ashes has already got the juice. It's just incredibly cool. The challenge for Greifenmaer  is to sustain its momentum and brings as much polish to bear on the gameplay and campaign as it has on the vibes. Optimizing the code so my middling PC has a chance of running it would also be nice.

The other new strategy title I went in-depth with at Games Ground was Steel Platoon - check out my first impressions here.

title: Rating the 2026 Warhammer Age of Sigmar Battleforce Boxes
content:
Games Workshop has prepared a selection of big honkin' Battleforces, just in time for the holidays. These are typically big collections of slightly older models, offered at a moderate discount and presenting a solid start to a new army, or a healthy expansion of an existing one. We'll break down each of these sets, figuring out how much you're saving, how useful they are, and roughly how many points they total up to.

Cities of Sigmar - Knights of Hammerhal ($255)

Contents:

  • 1 Tahlia Vedra, Lioness of the Parch
  • 1 Freeguild Cavalier-Marshal
  • 10 Freeguild Cavaliers

Contents MSRP: $376

Value saved: $121

Points Cost: 830

Finally, we get one for the horsegirls. The Cavalier-Marshal and 10 attendant Cavaliers are the backbone of a number of competitive lists right now, while also being beautiful models in their own right. There's a reason that Marshal shows up in so many Golden Daemon entries. Even taken in smaller, 5-horse units, the Cavaliers are great skirmishers and objective grabbers. Like a few of these sets, this one does have a big centerpiece named Hero who you can't really take two of. That said, if you don't already have Tahlia Vedra, she's an amazing centerpiece model and while spendy, is pretty useful in Cities of Sigmar armies. For new players this is a fun, if labor-intensive start, while established Cities players might not yet have this many Cavaliers in their stable.

Final Verdict: Buy, unless you already have Tahlia Vedra.

Nighthaunt - Court of the Undying King ($255)

Contents:

  • 1 Nagash
  • 2 Dreadblade Harrows
  • 10 Dreadscythe Harridans
  • 10 Bladegheist Revenants
  • 10 Grimghast Reapers

Contents MSRP: $368.75

Value saved: $113.75

Points Cost: 1450

This is a great start to a Nighthaunt army, giving you a solid core of infantry to build around. You're also not getting any Chainrasps, which most existing Nighthaunt players will already have at least a crypt's worth. The Dreadblade Harrows are kind of a weird thing to just throw in there, but the main attraction is obviously the biggest bone daddy with the biggest hat, Nagash. He's pretty hard to fit in a list, being 750 points at time of writing, but that does make this the single most points-heavy box across both the 40K and Age of Sigmar Battleforces. He's an older model so might not fit together quite as nicely as more recent releases, but is the kind of centerpiece that absolutely dominates the table. If you don't have him this is a great excuse to get one of the few bona fide main characters of Warhammer, but if you already have him haunting your cabinet, it's not like you can really use two.

Final Verdict: Buy, unless you already have Nagash.

Orruk Warclans - Grunta Stampede ($255)

Contents:

  • 2 Tuskboss on Maw-Grunta/Maw-Grunta Gouger/Maw-Grunta with Hakkin' Krew
  • 6 Gore Gruntas

Contents MSRP: $366

Value saved: $111

Points Cost: 790

The intended way to run this set is as a Tuskboss on Maw-Grunta and a Maw Grunta-Gouger, and the points value above reflects that. Big pigs haven't really been shaking up the competitive scene, and the base Gore Gruntas definitely lag behind their larger compatriots (Compigtriots? Hampatriots? Comporktriots? I'm trying too hard). From a competitive standpoint this isn't really a great box right now, but strictly on vibes, it's hard not to love this much commitment to one particular bit.

Final Verdict: Pass if you're trying to build a good competitive list, but go hog wild if you want some pigs.

Stormcast Eternals - Annihilation Host ($255)

Contents:

  • 1 Lord-Commander Bastian Carthalos
  • 1 Lord-Relictor
  • 1 Lord-Celestant
  • 3 Praetors
  • 9 Annihilators/Annihilators with Meteoric Grandhammers

Contents MSRP: $388.50

Value saved: $133.50

Points Cost: 920

This almost feels like clearing old stock; I haven't seen Praetors or Annihilators much since the Dominion box in 3rd edition, and they feel like a weird fit with these heroes. That said, we're fans of Bastian Carthalos here, and like with the Ironjawz box, this set commits to a bit. 9 Annihilators is a real "hell yeah" statement, and if you're leaning into that semi-meme list archetype, this box is great for that. The Lord-Relictor and Lord-Celestant are both fine but not especially exciting, and the Praetors are more useful giving your big dragon heroes a Ward save instead of anyone here. It probably should have had a Lord-Veritant who synergizes with Annihilators far better, but then it really would have just seemed like Dominion back stock.

Final Verdict: A firm maybe.

Slaves to Darkness - Legion of Damnation ($255)

Contents:

  • 1 Chaos Lord of Daemonic Mount/Eternus
  • 5 Chaos Chosen
  • 3 Varanguard
  • 5 Chaos Knights
  • 10 Chaos Warriors

Contents MSRP: $381.50

Value saved: $126.50

Points Cost: 1090

Is it crazy to suggest you buy two of these things? This is the definition of "all killer, no filler," only the "killer" refers to actual murderers. If you got two of this set, added a Sorcerer, and dropped one horsey hero you'd have a great competitive list. Everything here rules on the tabletop, and aside from the Varanguard, they're all fairly recent models that go together pretty easily. Even just taking one of this box, it's a great core to just about any list, and you're getting a lot of points for the money.

Final Verdict: Windmill slam that buy button.

Plaguesworn Host ($255)

Contents:

  • 1 Harbinger of Decay
  • 1 Lord of Blights
  • 3 Sloven Knights
  • 5 Putrid Blightkings
  • 10 Rotswords
  • 14 Pox Wretches
  • 6 Mire Kelpies

Contents MSRP: $364

Value saved: $109

Points Cost: 910

This is another great start to an army. You'll always be taking Rotswords and Pox Wretches, often take the Sloven Knights, and the rest are still useful, just not always part of your plan. It's a good mix of cheap little trash units and spendy chonkers. Ideally the Lord of Blights would instead be a Lord of Plagues, but on the bright side (Blight side? Ugh.) the Harbinger of Decay is probably the coolest model in the entire range. It's a box of usable, often staple stuff, and makes up almost half of a full army.

Final Verdict: A solid pick, but not quite a slam dunk.

Final Verdict

This batch of boxes often lean into some niche builds like Oops! All Annihilators or Big Pigs Over the Road Racing, but all offer some significant savings and higher points values than their 40K equivalents. The Slaves to Darkness box is probably the single best Battleforce across both games this holiday season, so if you were looking for an excuse to add a bunch of spiky jerks to your backlog, this just might be it.

title: Getting Started: Eldfall Chronicles
content:
Welcome back to another article about Eldfall Chronicles, the combination skirmish and dungeon crawl game from Freecompany. You might have seen some of our recent ongoing coverage here at Tabletop Battles and wondered what exactly it would take to try this game out. Good news, that's exactly what you're reading right now.

The first thing I'd suggest doing is figuring out how you want to play the game. I touched on some of the many ways to play Eldfall Chronicles earlier, but it mostly boils down to whether you want to play the skirmish wargame or the cooperative dungeon crawl. All of the models in the game can be used in either form of gameplay, but there definitely are some entry points that are smoother than others.

Eldfall Chronicles Imperial Banner. Credit: Blake Law

Also, as a reminder, Freecompany has all of the rules for everything available for free on their website. Whether you want the core rules for the skirmish wargame, dungeon crawl, or any other additional rules (like behavior cards, FAQs, competitive play quests, etc.) then you can find them on their Resources page. Additionally, there's an app called Guild Hall which is used for building forces in the skirmish game. Through this, you can view every model's rules, all the spells and upgrades in the game, and save your forces to be referenced later.

Enough website stuff. Let's start by looking at the dungeon crawl options because they're both very simple and quite timely!

Dungeon Crawling in Eldfall Chronicles

If you want to play one of the dedicated dungeon crawl experiences, it's pretty easy to make the recommendations for what to look for. There are currently two core boxes, each of which contains everything you need to play.

There are a lot of moving parts in the dungeon crawl games. Beyond the normal mechanics of playing the game, there are various decks of cards that have to be curated between games, some form of time tracking to ensure your party isn't lollygagging during their delving, and various other miscellaneous things to track that aren't present in the skirmish game. However, the structure of both campaigns starts out with some very stripped down tutorial missions that gradually add on more mechanics. For Northern Wind, you work through five different quests that each build on each other before having the full suite of mechanics in play. We don't have as many details about Apocrypha yet, but I can confirm there are at least two of these tutorial style missions that help ease you into everything.

An early quest in Northern Wind. Credit: Jake Bennington

Northern Wind

First up, and the only option if you want something right now, is Northern Wind. If you want a deeper look inside the box, Tabletop Battles has your back because we have a review of Northern Wind that covers the gameplay, contents, and more. We've also been playing through the game and recording our experiences in a series of battle reports, so check those out for more Northern Wind thoughts.

At $217, it sits at the price point for premium board games or things like Warhammer 40,000 Battleforce Boxes. For this price, you'll get a packed box that includes 15 miniatures (4 heroes, 6 undead, 5 oni), 30+ dungeon tiles, and a boatload of cards and tokens plus the various rulebooks to play. This is more than enough for hours of replayable gameplay as you take different routes up the mountain, make different choices, and (potentially) include different members of your party.

All of the included models also have their relevant skirmish profile cards included, but the only fully playable force you'd have from this box would be the oni. The heroes themselves are members of different factions, so while you can't necessarily field an opposing force for the oni, you would have some models that you could add to any of the other packs that are out there.

Goblin Wartribe. Credit: keewa

There are various expansion packs available, but they only expand what's already a very hefty amount of game. They range from single model releases that replace the cardboard standees (Oni Pariah, Oni Yaksha, Nekomata & Komainu, Kogetsu, Amazon Gladiatrix, and Guildsworn Knight) to expansions that add entirely new encounters or hero options. The Goblin Wartribes expansion in particular feels like a nice value because it provides a new set of enemies for Northern Wind, a fully playable faction for the skirmish game, and also an alternate hero option with Chanra the Goblin Shaman. The Blighted Riftspawn expansion serves as a massive final boss to be the capstone of a Northern Wind playthrough, so you could wait until you're a handful of sessions into the game before snagging this terror.

Apocrypha

The next option is Apocrypha, the latest release for Eldfall Chronicles. It's so new that it's still in crowd funding status over at Gamefound for the next two weeks. If you want to see what Apocrypha is like, we had a review go up just a few days ago. The cheapest point of entry is the Core Pledge level that is around $100 USD – this nets you the entire game including four hero miniatures and a miniature for the final boss with all the rest of the enemies being represented by cardboard standees. The astute among you will have noticed this price point is quite a bit lower than Northern Wind's. It's partly due to a crowd funding discount but also because this version of the core box was intended to be more of a board game feel with fewer miniatures and more standees which keeps the price down. The stretch goals have also been getting blasted through, so by the time this article goes live there are probably at least a few extra goodies that will be included.

Delving through the first mission in Act I of Apocrypha. Credit: Jake Bennington

There are, of course, different levels that offer different amounts of rewards. The Deluxe Pledge replaces all of the standees with miniatures (13 models) for around $230 USD. The Collector Pledge is about $290 USD and adds on an expansion pack of particularly cool looking undead that, like the Goblin Wartribes, are also going to be a playable faction in the skirmish game. There are even higher tier options that include everything plus a bunch of fancy swag like acrylic tokens, card sleeves, storage options, and the like.

And if you're a complete sicko (positive connotation), you can do the Dungeon-Crawl All-in and get everything ever released for Northern Wind and Apocrypha at once. If you do, let me know because I want to be your friend.

Dungeon Crawl Summary

If you're interested in playing the dungeon crawl format for Eldfall Chronicles, the short version is to either pick up Northern Wind or Apocrypha. Northern Wind is available right now and has a ton of gameplay to keep you occupied but even the cheapest price point is enough to make some folks pause. I think it's fully justified given how much stuff is in there, but it's 2026 and all. Apocrypha has an entry point of less than half the price, but it won't be delivered until approximately Q3 2027. Both games have a variety of additional add-ons and goodies you can pick up to further enhance it if you find yourself enjoying the base game.

Skirmishing in Eldfall Chronicles

A battle upon the ruins of the Sand Kingdoms. Credit: PierreTheMime

The skirmish game currently has a few different entry points, but that is going to be changing at some point in the near future. Let's take a look at what exists right now.

Two-Player Starter Sets

There are currently two different versions of the Two-Player Starter Sets. One contains models for the Empire of Soga (think samurai, Kitsune, and overall martial competency) vs Helian League (synergistic "elves" with a tendency for fire and high quality armaments). The other set pits the Coalition of Thenion (individualistic "elves" who specialize in hitting hard and fast) against the Sand Kingdoms (a desert-dwelling faction composed entirely of magic users). Both of these boxes contain most of the other components you'll need to play a game – rulebook, unit cards, tokens, and dice. There's even a bonus water elemental in each of these boxes. The only thing you will need in addition to these boxes is some type of terrain. Grab some existing terrain or just use some glasses, the boxes the models came in, and whatever is lying around to create an impromptu battle to get a feel for things.

I absolutely love that Freecompany shows stuff like this in their Quick Start Rules because it's absolutely how a lot of people get into games. Not everyone has a closet full of terrain! Credit: Freecompany

One nice thing about these two sets is that there are corresponding Quick Start Rules (available on the Resources page linked above) for each of them. These documents are just nine short pages each, but they walk you through a simplified introduction to the skirmish game involving just two models per side and only a handful of the rules. It's enough to get a feel for the game and prepare you for the full thing afterwards. I like how, despite this being Baby's First Eldfall, it isn't just a straightforward death match like a lot of games have. There's still an objective that both players are fighting over.

Single Faction Starter

The faction pack bundles from the two-player starters are also available separately – if you only want the Empire of Soga models but not the Helian League, you can pick them up by themselves. However, the price point makes a lot more sense if you can just split with someone interested in the other faction because all the tokens, dice, rules, and water elemental wind up just being free.

However, there are some factions that aren't available in those two player sets. These include the Goblin Wartribes and Oni Clans, so if those are the factions who speak to you (and you don't pick up the Northern Wind box which includes the Oni), then this is an option. As if those aren't enough options, each of the four core factions (Soga, Helian, Thenion, Sand Kingdoms) have what's called a Reinforcement Pack. These are 3 models for the faction and each contains two brand new units along with one resculpt of an existing model. It's handy because each of these alternate sculpts happens to be a model that can be taken more than once (and from my understanding are popular to do so with), so you can get some variety in your army lists even if taking duplicate models.

Eldfall Chronicles Sunspear Reinforcements. Credit: Blake Law

Future Starter Options

I mentioned the two-player skirmish introduction point is going to be changing in the future. This was straight from a community milestone Q&A video that came out a month ago. Instead of having two separate starter boxes, they're going to have a single entry point for skirmish. This is to have a unifying new player entry point and likely also reduces SKU bloat which is a problem all games face when stores start stocking them on shelves. It will be different from the ones currently on offer and will feature two new sub-factions (no, we don't quite know what that means yet). The existing models will stick around in their own, single faction releases as mentioned above.

Skirmish Summary

If all of the factions are equally interesting to you, I think the general consensus is to go for the Empire of Soga vs Helian League box. Those two factions are a little more straightforward than the squishy glass cannons of Thenion or the "everyone is a mage so I hope you like looking at the spell list" of Sand Kingdom. The Oni also just have so much raw power that they can carry a newer player through some learning games based solely on their stats.

There's nothing stopping you from using the Quick Start guides with other factions if those are the ones that you favor. There's also a Game Night Guide which is intended for someone running demos of the game, but could easily be used by two players learning the game themselves.

Blue and Red Rasetsu. Credit: Justin Crawford

Welcome To Calad!

Eldfall Chronicles is a crunchy game with a lot going on at any one time, but there are baby steps you can do to get familiar with it without having to jump into the deep end straight away. It's also a pretty neat feeling to know that if you're learning the rules to play in one format, they're basically identical to what you'd do to play the other ways and all of your models can freely swap between dungeon crawl and skirmish. How do you plan on exploring the world of Calad?

title: Games from the Crypt #26 - Bohn Again
content:
"It's about farming beans."

That was the pitch the vendor gave when I was looking at some imported card games at a convention back in 1997. Of course I furrowed my brow. Of course I looked at the dorky cartoon bean farmer on the cover and smirked. Of course I thought "how dumb is that." And of course I bought it.

Now, almost 30 years on, Uwe Rosenberg's Bohnanza remains an absolute crypt classic - a brilliantly designed card game with a particularly unusual hand management concept and intense player interaction by way of bean trading. Trust me, it is much more exciting than it sounds, and although the novelty of introducing it to a group and fielding the "WTF is this crap" reaction when you tell everyone they will be playing a game about harvesting legumes has worn off, the singularity and uniqueness of it have not.

Version 1.0.0

I recall reading the printed out English translation of the German rules - this was before Rio Grande Games had picked it up for US release - and having to explain and re-explain to my friends that once cards were dealt, you absolutely could not change or sort the order of the cards. This simple restriction broke many brains back in the day, but in order the game to work as it does it absolutely requires players to play the cards they have been given in the order they are given to them. This game is all about restrictions, working around them, and using limitations as a catalyst for tough decisions and trade incentives.

Once cards are dealt (and absolutely not rearranged), each player must play - or plant as the case may be -  the first card in their hand. This card will be one of many different bean types, which have varying rarity in the deck. The second card they may choose to play if they want. Then they flip over the top two cards of the deck and an open trading session begins, whereby players can trade cards from their hands with the active player for these face-up cards. Once trading is concluded, anything traded for must be planted immediately and the active player draws three cards. Again, not changing their order in any way.

You see, each player can only have two fields (i.e. rows or stacks), each containing a single type of bean. You can buy a third with gold if you so choose. The more beans that you have in a field, the more exponentially their value grows when it's time to harvest them and convert the cards into gold coins, shown on the back of the card. The rarer beans have higher values and need fewer cards to get into good money. So you might find yourself absolutely sweating over getting rid of a cheap and plentiful Weinbrandbohne through trade in order to keep your more lucrative Rote Bohne and Kakaobohne fields active and earning more money. You can also gift beans to clear out the trades, but it's much smarter to work out deals and fill your fields to max value. Because of course, the most gold at the end (once the deck has been run through twice) is the winner.

It's such a ingenious system that creates the impetus for high stakes trading as well as careful strategic planning. The only way you can manipulate your hand order and what you are going to be forced to play is by trading, and it is only through the trading that you can effectively get into the higher tiers of bean payouts. I love that it is such a silly theme, yet it's a game that engenders plenty of tension, bickering, debates, deals, and schadenfreude when someone is forced to plow up a valuable and growing field with lots of potential to plant garbage beans. There's a little bit of the classic card game Pit in its DNA, but it is much more structured and, well, Germanic.

Uwe Rosenberg would of course emerge as one of the premier game designers of the early 2000s with big, massive, and complex titles like Agricola and A Feast for Odin but I maintain that Bohnanza is still his finest design. It's a simple family card game released at the absolute peak of the golden age for German games It has a timeless that not even several frankly misguided and overwrought expansions that added pirates, a mini-wargame, mutants, a western theme, and too many bean-related puns have diminished. It is still in print, with a recent US edition published by Pandasaurus. It's same great game - mostly. The original artwork was so iconic that I can't imagine playing this game with "Jalapeno Joe" and not the Saubohne.

title: No, MTG Star Trek is not a Universes Beyond killer
content:
Magic: The Gathering had its Star Trek prereleases last week, and many fans and game stores have reported surprisingly low turnout, with events condensed down into fewer days or cancelled altogether.

While it's all anecdotes and there's a lack of any hard data to go off, it seems to be widely believed among the community that something went wrong with the Star Trek prerelease, and I've seen severalcreators comment on this.

I've also seen fans jumping to some absolutely wild conclusions off the back of this idea, saying that it proves Universes Beyond was a mistake all along, or that Wizards of the Coast will surely pivot away from third-party tie-ins right away. And, of course, it doesn't and won't.

First of all, and I doubt this is breaking news to many of you, one bad Universes Beyond set is not going to make Wizards of the Coast give up on the idea. Not when smash-hits like Final Fantasy and Lord of the Rings have shown they can milk popular IPs to make more money than God. You don't slay your golden goose because it lays one normal egg.

Pulling back on Universes Beyond due to a single failure would be incredibly reactionary and just downright foolish, like stopping all Standard sets altogether after a dud, or responding to Nadu being broken by scrapping all Simic cards (Well hold on, we might have something there.).

Crucially, Magic: The Gathering sets take a lot of time to make, and at any one time Wizards has a few year's worth of releases in the pipeline. That means it naturally responds to customer trends slowly. This is why we saw so many smaller sets like Assassin's Creed after March of the Machine: Aftermath rotted on store shelves. Even if Wizards decided to stop tie-ins today, we'd still get Universes Beyond sets for roughly the next three years.

So, no, Wizards won't be pulling back the intensity of UB releases. What it might do, if MTG Star Trek does indeed turn out to be a flop, is think a little differently about which franchises it takes on for a tentpole set. Perhaps it isn't enough for an IP to be a huge household name and have sufficient concepts to fill out the different colors and required cards for a Magic set. You also need to think about audience demographics, and (since Star Trek means different things to different people) how cohesive an IP is.

However, it is far too early to call MTG Star Trek a failure. Firstly, there's only anecdotal evidence that interest is low, and obviously that's pretty weak. How many times have we been surprised by WotC revealing that a supposed flop actually outperformed expectations?

Secondly, even if prerelease numbers were down, this doesn't necessarily mean Star Trek will sell badly. This set's audience will naturally skew older and my assumption is that often this older demographic is usually not the one attending in-store events. While Star Trek may not be very good for stores, there could still be a sizable enough fan base purchasing packs for it to be considered a success.

I particularly think the Star Trek precons will do well. This franchise, like Doctor Who, is very fragmented, with different groups of fans caring greatly about some eras of the show, and entirely cold on the rest. Just like Doctor Who, while the main set has everything mashed up together, the Star Trek precons allow you to only engage with the parts of the franchise that you particularly enjoy. TOS fans have their own box, and fans of the other classic series are well catered to with Federation Fleet, while regular Magic players can be seduced by all the artifact synergies within the Borg.

We need to wait until we have some actual information to draw any conclusions about how Star Trek has performed. And even if this were the worst set in the history of Magic (which I highly doubt) that won't suddenly outweigh Universes Beyond's many successes. Like it or not, UB is here to stay for the foreseeable future.

Come join the conversation over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Warhound Mail Bag: Running Disruption in Singles and Teams
content:
In today's subscribers only piece, Lowest of Men tackles the thorny issue of Disruption, the oft maligned fifth disposition, and how you can get the most out of it in singles and teams. Enjoy!

Otakunomike: what faction is best equipped to play Disruption, for both teams and the crazy solo players doing it because they can?

Thanks very much for your question, Otakunomike! Disruption is well known as the 'struggler' of the five dispositions in the early stages of 11th edition. Usually the last choice for teams and singles, we have nonetheless seen some lists getting the most out of it. It is imperative you get your Disruption choice right (especially in Teams!) so that it doesn't become a deadweight and undo the work your strongest lists are doing elsewhere.

I want to break down what makes a Disruption list tick in some detail, before considering armies and builds that do it well, and why. Let's get into it!

Disruption: The Problem

Ultimately, Disruption is an unusual disposition because many of its missions are shaped around what the opposing disposition does, and as such it does not have a 'single' character mission wise. This means the demands on it are more varied than many of the other dispositions. It also struggles a little on the relative weighting of 'passive scoring' against other dispositions in some match ups. For more detail on this, see our guide to the disposition match ups from release.

Having said that, there are some consistent demands and features for a Disruption list that I think hold true across archetypes:

  1. Action Economy. Several of the Disruption missions require multiple disposable action units for building up early score. Whether through setting Death Traps, pushing buttons against Priority Assets, or setting up tokens against Recon, Disruption is a 'busy' disposition - the taller, greedier lists of 11th Edition are not naturally good at doing this. You have to have some disposable idiots!
  2. Teeth. To put it mildly, Disruption players are targeted in teams and singles by greedy lists on better scoring dispositions. You need to PUNISH this by having adequate damage and guile in the list to capitalise on an enemy trying to wrack up a score. Balancing the cute scoring pieces with enough damage to cripple the enemy and win the game is crucial, and this can also help you push to overcome a poor scoring match up by simply, ya know, tabling the enemy too.
  3. Board Control. As we will discuss in a moment, there are various ways we are seeing this achieved out in the wild. But Disruption missions want you to establish and maintain a key grip on areas of the board that vary mission to mission. You either want a strong castle that is simply going to dominate your chosen areas, or the ability to flexibly relocate in mid to late game to get to where the last mission tokens are against Priority Assets, or to score kills on your Death Traps, etc.

So which factions can achieve this? There are two main ways to look at this. The cute, and the brutal. Let's start with the techy stuff before moving to some of our killier heavy hitters!

Disruption: The Cute Approach

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

One way to play Disruption is the capitalise on the relative lack of units and screening in many top builds (especially Take and Hold / Purge the Foe), to exploit uppy downy antics, relocating units, and the ability to hit and fight on your terms. The two standout builds that do this are:

Chaos Space Marines (Warpstrike Champions) and Tyranids (Subterranean Assault).

How do they do this? Both exploit a similar set of tools. They have disposable idiots for actions early on - Lictors and the like for the 'Nids, Chaos Bikers, Cultists and Raptors for the CSM.

After that, comes the relocating damage - this marries together that need for flexible board control with the need to brutalise / preferably table the opponent, especially if they over-extend. Both armies can uppy downy some great shooting and melee units, and they have good ways to deliver this damage into new areas every turn. This allows them to hit weak spots, chase the parts of the board the mission scoring requires them to be in, and exploit gaps in the opposing lines.

The Red Terror by Sky Serpent

Does it work? Sometimes... Both these builds are super expressive and fun to play, and can punish mistakes. Neither army is easy to push into in a teams sense. That said, they can find themselves running out of space and assets in certain games, and that's when they risk being blown out. You want to know your matrix and win conditions in teams very well, as well as what boards you can get the space to play on and exploit your opponent's weaknesses.

We can also give a mention to Adepta Sororitas lists running Disruption here. The idea here is you have a wall of idiots in the form of Dominions and Immolators to play early game, before a castle of Vahl / Paragons and additional tanks and even more Paragons follows up with a vengenace to convert the win. It isn't quite as technical as the lists above, but it has better and more consistent damage ceilings and a greater width of damage units as well. Overall, that makes it an underexplored stand out in this category.

I know what you're thinking. Tom, shouldn't GSC, Aeldari, and Drukhari also be good at this style of cute Disruption play?! And the answer is, they're not awful at it. Astra Militarum have also had a crack at it in recent times too. You have the scoring and the speed, and you can apply some damage when pushed. But particularly for teams play right now these sorts of frail and interesting armies appear to be languishing somewhat as GW sells industrial quantities of Terminators and Outriders to the masses. I'd bet good money on these armies, and Disruption in general, becoming an absolute terror once more codices emerge later in the edition and more balance passes have been made...

Disruption: The Brutal Approach

Credit: Dan Dayon

Ok, enough with the cute. Let's look at some beefier takes on Disruption. Being strong and solid and pushing out after the enemy rebounds from you is a pretty consistent win path in 11th, and some of the best Disruption lists have leant hard into this. The two main standouts are as follows:

Necrons (Obeisance Phalanx / Pharoah's Armour) and Death Guard (Shamblerot Vectorum / Paragons of Putrescance)

Although radically different lists, there are some similarities in these two builds, that are both playing to out attrition the opponent with several big centrepieces that render the missions for Disruption relatively easy. The Phalanx Necrons pack a Tesseract Vault, the Silent King, an Obelisk, and sometimes even C'tan on top for a classic Necron stat check. They compliment that with enough scoring junk to round out the game - it is worth saying the Titanic Necron units can action and shoot here which makes their action economy better than it first appears.

Norman's Mortarion

The Death Guard does similar, with a castle of Mortarion / Defiler / Knight Despoiler backed up by hordes of Zombies (including free reserves ones via the detachment) and a bit of Plague Marine or Plaguecaster MSU and Rhinos. Where the Necrons are leaning on AoC and -1 damage defensive strats alongside their regeneration, the Death Guard have the ability to pass off wounds to Poxwalkers and to leverage Mortarion's shoot back aura to force very difficult engagements for the opponent early game, until it's too late and they stand astride the middle triumphant.

These two builds have seen more consistent success than the 'cute' archetypes because, well, there's nothing cute about 11th edition in it's current form. Standing in the middle and being more durable than your opponent is carrying the day at the moment. Both have benefitted from being teched 'just enough' for Disruption, but mostly being a list designed to absorb and then body the opponent, winning the military battle.

What Next?

It is worth briefly highlighting from a teams perspective that we are seeing some initial experimentation with Disruption in Space Marines - you can still get an incredible points efficient, pushy army with tanks, Outriders, Gulliman and Terminator shooting that will run through opposing armies whilst pushing the buttons required in the missions as well. Time will tell if these hold up, but it does raise the possibility your team might just want a powerful list built to table the opponent over the Disruption centred builds. We will see!

Thanks very much for your question, and for supporting Tabletop Battles. We will be back with more subscribers only content very soon!

Lowest of Men, out.

content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Back to normal this week wth a healthy crop of events, and there's a bit of movement at the top. Dark Angels loom ominously over the metagame, which is not much of a surprise, but we've had huge surges for the Adepta Sororitas and Iron Hands in pursuit, as both factions find solid ways to adapt to the metagame. The World Championships of Warhammer loom ever closer too, and with the release of the FAQ for that last week, the stage should be set for people to conduct final testing. Let's see what's going on out there.

Black Templars also had a bit of a breakout week, albeit at fairly low player counts, and Celeste does a sterling job here of leading the charge. Thoughts

The crowd is chanting "Quad-o-Saur, Quad-o-Saur", and you better believe that one of the most brutal Ork builds we've yet seen is stepping onto the table. God it must have been so viscerally satisfying to realise fit in 2000pts. It's a total nightmare for anyone else, but you have to admire the beauty of it.

The Sisters are going to try and do more than that, of coruse, aiming to turn the hunt back on the greenskins. This...is not going to go super well. Normally you'd fancy Sisters to have a decent go at a matchup like this, as multi-meltas and Vahl are ideal tools for it, but the Sisters are light on those pieces (including no Vahl, very rare) in favour of more balanced board control. Good for some matchups, absolutely the last thing you want here - the Orks can bully the Sororitas something fierce, and have the speed to make that extremely problematic very quickly. I imagine if you're in the Sisters shoes here you look at the split flamer/melta Retributor squad in your army and just start crying. The fact that almost all the big threats have a Feel No Pain just adds insult to injury, as even if you do push some melta shots through, they can still spike through it.

Anything the Sororitas can do? The Triumph squad can be somewhat annoying, and maybe grab a point for longer than you might think, though has to watch out for Ghaz coming and ripping them apart with Precision. Really and truly, to win here the Sisters need both Repentia squads to fully pop off and cleanly lift a priority target each, and then maybe this is a game (albeit still very uphill). Odds of that feel nowhere near high enough, and a brutal trampling is the expected (and actual) outcome here.

title: Warhammer 40k lore - are the servants of Nurgle genuinely happy?
content:
Few foes in the Warhammer 40,000 universe are as viscerally disgusting as the rotting, fungus-infested, parasitized, disease-ridden wretches bound to the service of Nurgle, Lord of Decay, the Grandfather, Chaos God of Disease and Despair. Yet despite existing in a state of continuous undying decay, Nurgle's mortal servants often rejoice in their pestilence, perceiving their weeping sores, sweltering fevers, and rancid buboes as signs of the Grandfather's favor. Are they genuinely having a good time, or are they just insane?

The most prominent Warhammer 40k faction associated with Nurgle is the Death Guard. The Death Guard served the Emperor in the Great Crusade as the XIVth Space Marine Legion, but gradually fell into the service of the plague god through the machinations of seventh captain Callas Typhon. Examining their fall is illuminating.

Laughing in relief

Callas Typhon was inducted into the dark secrets of the Chaos Gods by Chaplain Erebus of the Word Bearers, becoming the leader of the secret Seven Pillared Lodge, a warrior society within the Death Guard legion that subverted the Imperial structures of control. The Death Guard prided themselves on indomitability, enduring the unendurable, and the teachings of the Seven Pillared Lodge promised endurance even beyond the Legion's already superhuman limits.

Typhon delved deeper into the secrets of the warp, and ultimately betrayed the Legion as it made for the final siege of the Emperor's Palace on Terra. The Death Guard fleet was becalmed in the warp and unable to move when Typon summoned the Destroyer Plague, a supernatural disease that caused the Death Guard to decay and suffer without ever allowing them to die. As well as physical suffering beyond the limits that any mortal could bear, the Death Guard's pride was utterly destroyed - here was a challenge they truly could not endure.

The Primarch Mortarion struck a bargain with the plague god Nurgle to release his legion from their torment. The Destroyer Plague retreated into the body and soul of Typhon, remaking him as its host, Typhus. The rest of the Legion was 'blessed' by the Lord of Plagues. Their bodies were transformed beyond all reckoning into living vectors of sickness and corruption, but they felt no pain, experienced no weakness, and regained their sense of sense - but their perspectives had been greatly altered.

This shows one reason why Nurgle's mortal servants seem so happy. Nurgle's gifts don't cure diseases, but they do bring an end to suffering. For the downtrodden serfs of the Imperium, among whom malnutrition, injury, and disease are endemic and the only reprieve is faith in a distant Emperor, Nurgle's gifts offer an anaesthetic; for Typhon and the Death Guard, they provided a well of supernatural power fitting to their hubristic ambitions.

False consciousness

Mentally enduring Nurgle's gifts requires an altered perspective. Some, like Typhon, have the insane egocentrism needed to consciously accept the gifts. But Nurgle's presence alters the mind as much as the body.

In Siege of Terra: Warhawk by Chris Wraight, the White Scars lead an assault on the Death Guard at the Lion's Gate Space Port. The Primarch Jaghatai Khan manages to banish the Daemon Primarch Mortarion to the warp. Mortarion's banishment is like a sinking ship that pulls down smaller vessels with it, causing the influence of Nurgle to recede - without the grandfather's clammy embrace, many of the Death Guard are suddenly disquieted by their transformations, cut adrift.

In Dark Imperium: Plague War by Guy Haley, Roboute Guilliman begins an assault on a Death Guard position protected by a warp shield. To breach it and allow troops to insert, the primarch launches a rare cache of pariah missiles, each filled with the refined remains of dead psychic blanks. The explosive burst of anti-psychic energy has a devastating effect on the Death Guard, making some react to their bodies as if they have suddenly come to their senses, descending into despair and madness at their ruined forms.

Accepting the inevitable

Truly accepting the gifts of Nurgle means accepting the inevitability of decay and welcoming it as a sign of endurance. This is, in some ways, an exaggerated extension of accepting the natural aging process - like coming to terms with a middle aged beer gut, the fact that you don't run as fast as you used to, or even the fact that you have more achievements than ambitions. It is comfortable decay.

The novel Lords of Silence by Chris Wraight uses Nurgle to explore this middle-aged comfort from multiple angles. It takes place in the immediate aftermath of the opening of the Great Rift, with the Imperium unable to muster effective responses to Chaos raids. The protagonist Lord Vorx is faced with the philosophical question of what it may mean to have won the great struggle that defined his life, a profoundly middle-aged concern.

Meanwhile, the captive planetary defense force captain Dantine is enslaved by Vorx's warband, the Lords of Silence. Dantine finds himself face to face with an abominable enemy yet unable to fight, and his captors are surprisingly mellow.

He experiences the fall to Nurgle as letting go, relaxing from the Imperial web of performance and obligations such as his duty or maintaining his physical appearance: he learns to let it all hang out like someone middle-aged letting go of their vanity. Nurgle's corruption is easeful, which makes it a radical proposition for Imperials expected to live to their fullest (wherever they are within the Imperial hierarchy) and then abruptly die in duty.

Ultimately, people are complicated, and the precise parameters of the Chaos gods are changeable according to the whims of writers. Whether or not the mortal servants of Nurgle are genuinely happy, magically deluded, or living in a psychological false consciousness depends on the author writing them and what they want to achieve in a story.

Daemons of Nurgle

The question of whether the daemons of Nurgle are happy or not is actually very simple - we have categorical answers for every type except for Daemon Princes. Daemon Princes were once individual mortals, and though their souls are now fully absorbed within the great psychic gestalt that constitutes Nurgle, their minds are their own.

Nurglings are giggling and malicious imps with only limited sentience, but they're extremely happy. Plaguebearers, tasked with counting things for the grandfather - usually diseases, but ultimately anything they cast their single rheumy eye across - are morose, since their task is never-ending and constantly interrupted.

This changes if they contract the Chortling Murrain, which forces them to ceaselessly laugh, dance, and jig. They spend the next phase of their existence as a Sloppity Bilepiper, a mad jigging dance-master, before finally falling to pieces - at which point the next Bilepiper will put their head on a stick to use as a marotter puppet.

Beasts of Nurgle are puppylike entities that are enthusiastic and playful, bounding across battlefields to find new friends to play with. Unfortunately they tend to kill any mortals they contact, crushing them to death with their huge bulk or infecting them with withering plagues. This constant disappoint eventually dims their spirits. They will retreat to the Garden of Nurgle and enter a cocoon, finally emerging as a bitter and spiteful Rotfly.

The mighty Great Unclean ones are almost all avuncular, jolly, generous bestowers of Nurgle's gifts, mimicking their maker's gregarious nature. The one exception is Ku'Gath Plaguefather, Nurgle's favorite servant. Ku'gath was once a Nurgling until he fell into Nurgle's cauldron of plagues, accidentally imbibing the masterwork plague that Nurgle was brewing. Ku'gath swelled up into his new divine form, but he is so guilty and remorseful for destroying the Grandfather's great work that he now exists in a constant state of depressed contrition. He diverts all his efforts to brewing new plagues in an attempt to make recompense for his mistake.

Got a niche Warhammer lore question you'd like answered? Let me know in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: MTG and D&D workers hit back on Hasbro CEO's "anti-union comments"
content:
United Wizards of the Coast lambasted Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks on Bluesky, pushing back on comments the business leader made during an on-stage interview with The WBUR Breakfast Club.

"I think we're in support of a person's right to unionize and a person's right to have the discussion around it and a vote around it," said Chris Cocks, before pointing out there are "a fair number of people who don't want to be part of the union".

"It affects everyone. If 60 percent of the people on a team want to unionise, 100 percent of the people have to join the union and have to join collective bargaining," he said and followed up with a defence of Wizards of the Coast's working conditions, which he argued were better than average in the games industry. (It's about the 16:40 minute mark in the video below.)

However, on Bluesky the United Wizards of the Coast shot back at what it considered "incorrect and clearly anti-union" statements.

The union argued that members' wages were lower than the $140,000 average Chris Cocks claimed and said "there's no clear path toward promotions and meaningful raises."

Unionization efforts have provided opportunities for WotC staff to compare compensation. "We've seen workers with the same title with wildly different salaries, critical work going undercompensated, and stagnant career paths where members go unpromoted year after year".

The United WotC account also pointed to Hasbro's use of Fisher Phillips in the proceedings, which it claims is a "union avoidance" firm, as a sign that it is not in support of the right to unionize as Cocks has claimed.

"Unions are how tabletop workers ensure that we are treated with the respect that we deserve. We want to continue making the games we love. When we hold our union election, we believe we will win and take the first steps toward a better Wizards of the Coast."

The WotC union vote is set to take place later today, on November 10.
